meta.title: Arithmetic Progressions
meta.source_edition: NCERT Reprint 2026-27, Class 10 Mathematics, Ch 5 (jemh105.pdf, printed pages 49-72)

board_asks: finding the nth term (or which term / how many terms), the sum of the first n terms, and modelling a real situation as an AP -- these three carry almost every mark here.

big_idea.tagline: Add the same step, again and again.
big_idea.body: An arithmetic progression is a list of numbers where each term is the previous one plus a fixed step $d$ (the common difference). Pin down just two numbers -- the first term $a$ and the common difference $d$ -- and the whole list is fixed: $a,\ a+d,\ a+2d,\dots$. The chapter answers three questions: what is the nth term? ($a_n = a+(n-1)d$), which term / how many terms? (solve that formula for $n$), and what is the sum of the first n terms? ($S_n = \dfrac{n}{2}[2a+(n-1)d]$).

definitions.verbatim: So, an arithmetic progression is a list of numbers in which each term is obtained by adding a fixed number to the preceding term except the first term.
definitions.plain: A running list where you reach the next number by adding the SAME fixed amount every time. To test a list, check that consecutive differences are all equal.

definitions.verbatim: This fixed number is called the common difference of the AP. Remember that it can be positive, negative or zero.
definitions.plain: $d = a_{k+1} - a_k$ -- subtract any term from the one AFTER it (not before). The sign of $d$ tells you whether the AP rises ($d>0$), falls ($d<0$) or stays flat ($d=0$).

definitions.verbatim: a, a + d, a + 2d, a + 3d, . . . represents an arithmetic progression where a is the first term and d the common difference. This is called the general form of an AP.
definitions.plain: Every AP is captured by two numbers: the first term $a$ and the common difference $d$. Know those and you can write the whole list.

definitions.verbatim: So, the nth term an of the AP with first term a and common difference d is given by an = a + (n – 1) d.
definitions.plain: $a_n = a + (n-1)d$ -- take $(n-1)$ steps of size $d$ from the first term. This single formula answers 'find the 20th term', 'which term is 78?', and 'how many terms?' (rearrange for $n$).

definitions.term: Sum of the first n terms
definitions.verbatim: So, the sum of the first n terms of an AP is given by S = n/2 [2a + (n – 1) d]
definitions.plain: $S_n = \dfrac{n}{2}[2a+(n-1)d]$. If the last term $l$ is already known, the shortcut $S_n = \dfrac{n}{2}(a+l)$ is faster. Note $S_n$ needs the number of terms $n$, not a term's value.

source.note: printed stacked fraction n/2 linearised as n/2 with brackets

definitions.verbatim: Each of the numbers in the list is called a term.
Note that in examples (a) to (e) above, there are only a finite number of terms. Such an AP is called a finite AP.
The APs in examples (i) to (v) in this section, are not finite APs and so they are called infinite Arithmetic Progressions. Such APs do not have a last term.
an is also called the general term of the AP. If there are m terms in the AP, then am represents the last term which is sometimes also denoted by l.
If a, b, c are in AP, then b = (a + c)/2 and b is called the arithmetic mean of a and c.

concepts.title: Recognise an AP
concepts.body: A list is an AP only if the gap between consecutive terms is constant: $a_2-a_1 = a_3-a_2 = \dots = d$. Compute one or two differences before assuming -- squares ($1,4,9,\dots$) and doubling lists ($2,4,8,\dots$) are the classic traps that look regular but are NOT APs.
concepts.tested: MCQ / 'which of these forms an AP'

concepts.title: The nth term
concepts.body: $a_n = a + (n-1)d$. Read off the first term $a$ and common difference $d$, then substitute the position $n$. This is the most-used tool in the chapter.

concepts.title: Sum of the first n terms
concepts.body: $S_n = \dfrac{n}{2}[2a+(n-1)d]$, or $\dfrac{n}{2}(a+l)$ when the last term $l$ is known. The formula links four quantities $S_n, a, d, n$ -- given any three you can find the fourth.

concepts.title: Solve for n -- which term / how many terms
concepts.body: Set $a_n$ (or $S_n$) equal to the target value and solve for $n$. $n$ MUST come out a positive integer -- a fractional or negative $n$ means the value is simply not a term of the AP. A sum condition gives a quadratic in $n$, which can yield two valid answers.

concepts.title: Model a real situation as an AP
concepts.body: A fixed-increment salary, uniform monthly savings, rows of plants decreasing by a constant, a penalty rising by a fixed step -- extract the first term $a$ and the constant change $d$, then apply the term or the sum formula. Reject any answer the situation forbids (you cannot have a fractional number of rows).

examples.shape: Find the nth term . NCERT Example 3
examples.problem_verbatim: Find the 10th term of the AP : 2, 7, 12, . . .

solution_steps.lead: Read off a, d, n and write the formula.

examples.mark_logic: 2-mark shape (Section B): 1 for the correct data + formula $a_n=a+(n-1)d$, 1 for the signed substitution and the answer.

examples.shape: Which term is -81? Is any term 0? . NCERT Example 4
examples.problem_verbatim: Which term of the AP : 21, 18, 15, . . . is – 81? Also, is any term 0? Give reason for your answer.

solution_steps.lead: Now test whether any term equals 0.
solution_steps.text: Put $a_n = 0$: $21 + (n-1)(-3) = 0 \Rightarrow 3(n-1) = 21 \Rightarrow n = 8$. So the eighth term is $0$.

examples.mark_logic: 3-mark shape (Section C): 1 for the equation from $a_n=a+(n-1)d$, 1 for solving to $n=35$, 1 for the second part ($n=8$, so the 8th term is 0). $n$ must be a positive integer -- that is the 'give reason' the question wants.

examples.shape: Sum of first n terms . NCERT Example 11
examples.problem_verbatim: Find the sum of the first 22 terms of the AP : 8, 3, –2, . . .

solution_steps.lead: Read off a, d, n and write the sum formula.

examples.mark_logic: 2-mark shape (Section B): 1 for the data + formula $S_n=\frac{n}{2}[2a+(n-1)d]$, 1 for the signed substitution and the answer $-979$.

examples.shape: How many terms give a required sum . NCERT Example 13
examples.problem_verbatim: How many terms of the AP : 24, 21, 18, . . . must be taken so that their sum is 78?

solution_steps.lead: Reduce to a quadratic in n.
Read off n -- both roots are valid.
solution_steps.text: $n = 4$ or $n = 13$; both are admissible, so the number of terms is either $4$ or $13$ (the terms from the 5th to the 13th sum to zero).

examples.mark_logic: 3-mark shape (Section C): 1 for the sum equation, 1 for reducing to $n^2-17n+52=0$, 1 for both admissible values $n=4$ or $13$. Reporting only one value is the classic lost mark.

examples.shape: Word problem -- how many rows . NCERT Example 10
examples.problem_verbatim: In a flower bed, there are 23 rose plants in the first row, 21 in the second, 19 in the third, and so on. There are 5 rose plants in the last row. How many rows are there in the flower bed?

solution_steps.lead: Model the rows as an AP.
solution_steps.text: The counts $23, 21, 19, \dots, 5$ form an AP with $a = 23$, $d = 21 - 23 = -2$, and last term $a_n = 5$.

solution_steps.lead: Solve for the number of rows.
solution_steps.text: $-18 = (n-1)(-2) \Rightarrow n - 1 = 9 \Rightarrow n = 10$. So there are $10$ rows in the flower bed.

examples.mark_logic: 3-mark shape (Section C): 1 for recognising the AP and reading $a$, $d$, last term; 1 for the equation $5 = 23 + (n-1)(-2)$; 1 for solving to $n = 10$ rows (a count, so a positive integer).

examples.shape: Multi-part word problem -- production . NCERT Example 16
examples.problem_verbatim: A manufacturer of TV sets produced 600 sets in the third year and 700 sets in the seventh year. Assuming that the production increases uniformly by a fixed number every year, find : (i) the production in the 1st year (ii) the production in the 10th year (iii) the total production in first 7 years

solution_steps.lead: Model production as an AP and use the two given terms.
solution_steps.text: Let $a_n$ be the sets made in year $n$. Uniform increase means an AP. Given $a_3 = 600$ and $a_7 = 700$: $\;a + 2d = 600$ and $a + 6d = 700$.
Subtracting: $4d = 100 \Rightarrow d = 25$, and $a = 550$. So the production in the 1st year is $550$.

solution_steps.lead: (iii) Set up the sum for the first 7 years.

examples.mark_logic: 5-mark shape (Section D): 1 for modelling + the two equations, 1 for solving to $a=550$ (part i), 1 for $a_{10}=775$ (part ii), 1 for the sum set-up, 1 for $S_7 = 4375$ (part iii). Each of the three parts carries its own credit.

strategies.cue: Given a list -- is it an AP?
strategies.text: Check the differences: $a_2-a_1$, $a_3-a_2$. Equal every time means AP with that value as $d$; one mismatch means it is not.
Set $a_n$ (or $S_n$) equal to the target and solve for $n$. $n$ must be a positive integer.
$S_n = \dfrac{n}{2}[2a+(n-1)d]$; if the last term $l$ is known, $S_n = \dfrac{n}{2}(a+l)$ is quicker.
Pull the first term $a$ and the fixed change $d$ from the situation, apply the term or sum formula, then reject any impossible answer.

pitfalls.text: Subtracting the wrong way for $d$ -- always (later term $-$ earlier term). For $6, 3, 0, -3, \dots$ the common difference is $-3$, not $+3$.
Confusing a term's value with its position $n$ -- 'which term is 78?' asks for $n$, not for a value.
Putting a term value where $n$ belongs inside $S_n = \dfrac{n}{2}[2a+(n-1)d]$ -- the sum formula uses the number of terms.
Forgetting $n$ must be a positive integer -- a fractional or negative $n$ means the number is NOT a term of the AP.
Mixing the two sum forms -- $\dfrac{n}{2}[2a+(n-1)d]$ needs $a$ and $d$; $\dfrac{n}{2}(a+l)$ needs the last term $l$.

third_tab_content.name: Sum of the first n terms -- where the formula comes from
third_tab_content.intro: NCERT motivates the sum formula with Gauss's schoolboy trick (p.63): to add 1 to 100 he wrote the list forwards, then backwards, and added the two lines so every column gave the same total 101. The same reversal turns the sum of ANY AP into n identical pairs -- that is the whole derivation.

steps.claim: Write the sum of the first n terms.
Write the same sum again, terms reversed.
Add the two lines term by term -- each of the n column-pairs gives the same total.
steps.justification: First+last, second+second-last, and so on each equal 2a + (n-1)d.

steps.claim: Regroup a + (n-1)d as the last term to get the a-and-l form.
steps.justification: Useful when the first term a and last term l are known but d is not (NCERT form (4), p.64).

source.note: Gauss motivation on p.63; the reversal derivation and both forms on p.64 (Summary points 4-5, p.72)

fig_ap_number_line.caption: An AP on the number line -- every hop adds the same common difference d
fig_ap_number_line.legend: Terms a, a+d, a+2d, . . . sit at equal gaps of d. A constant hop is exactly what makes a list an AP; change the hop and it stops being one.
